sources.fact: Kobayashi, Kikuchi and Okamura, PLoS ONE 4(7): e6256 (2009), 'Imaging of ultraweak spontaneous photon emission from human body displaying diurnal rhythm': the human body emits ultraweak visible light 1000 times lower than the sensitivity of our naked eyes; imaged with a cryogenic CCD camera; emission linked to changes in energy metabolism

National Geographic (Ed Yong, Jul 20, 2009): Kobayashi recruited five volunteers; camera sensitive to a single photon; glow a thousand times less intense than the sensitivity of the human eye; strongest in the late afternoon; faces are the shiniest parts of the body, mouths and cheeks especially; light comes from chemical reactions that produce free radicals
NBC News, 'Humans glow in visible light': five healthy male volunteers; emission lowest at 10 a.m. and peaking at 4 p.m.; faces glowed more than the rest of the body; tied to metabolic rhythms

math.note: National Geographic and NBC News: five volunteers
PLoS ONE abstract: 1000 times lower than the sensitivity of the naked eye
NBC News: peak at 4 p.m. (16:00), National Geographic: late afternoon

post.instagram_caption:
You are glowing. Right now ✨

In 2009, scientists in Japan filmed five volunteers with a camera that can catch single particles of light. The human body gives off visible light, about 1,000 times too weak for your eyes to see. They link it to metabolism. It was brightest around 4 pm, dimmest around 10 am, and brightest of all on the face.

So you are a firefly. Just a very, very dim one.

Sources: Kobayashi et al., PLoS ONE (2009); National Geographic; NBC News.
